What is force?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Whenever you push a door open, pull a bucket of water from a well, or kick a football, you are applying a force. Force can do several things: it can make a stationary object start to move, make a moving object stop, change the direction of a moving object, or change the shape of an object, like squeezing a piece of foam. The unit of force is the newton, written as N, named after the scientist Isaac Newton. You cannot see a force itself, but you can see what it does. So whenever something starts, stops, speeds up, slows down, turns, or changes shape, a force is responsible.

What are the types of force?

Forces are grouped into two main types: contact forces and non-contact forces. CONTACT forces act only when two objects touch. Examples are the push you give a wheelbarrow, friction that slows a sliding object, and tension in a rope during a tug-of-war. NON-CONTACT forces act without touching, across a gap. Examples are gravity, which pulls everything towards the earth even from a distance; magnetic force, which pulls or pushes magnets and iron objects; and electrostatic force between charged objects, like the way a rubbed biro attracts small bits of paper. A simple test: if the objects must touch for the force to act, it is a contact force; if it works across empty space, it is a non-contact force.

What is friction and is it useful or harmful?

Friction is a force that opposes motion between two surfaces that are in contact. It acts in the opposite direction to the way an object is moving, slowing it down. Friction is both useful and harmful. It is USEFUL because it lets us walk without slipping, lets car tyres and brakes grip the road, and lets us hold objects and strike a matchstick. It is HARMFUL because it wears out machine parts, shoe soles and tyres, and it produces unwanted heat, wasting energy. We increase friction when we need grip, for example by using rough soles, and we reduce it when it wastes energy, for example by oiling a bicycle chain. So friction is a friend when we need control and a nuisance when it wastes energy.

What is energy?

Energy is the ability to do work. Anything that can make something happen, such as moving an object, giving light, producing sound, or heating something, has energy. You get energy from the food you eat, which lets your body move and work. A moving danfo has energy, a burning firewood gives out energy as heat and light, and a stretched catapult stores energy ready to launch a stone. The unit of energy is the joule, written as J. Energy comes in many forms, and one of the most important facts in science is that energy is never destroyed; it only changes from one form to another. Without energy, nothing in the world could move, grow or work. That is why energy is so important to life.

What are the forms of energy?

Energy exists in several forms. Some important ones are: mechanical energy, the energy of moving or stretched objects, like a rolling tyre or a drawn bow; heat energy, which flows from hot to cold things, like the heat from a cooking fire; light energy, which lets us see, from the sun or a bulb; sound energy, produced by vibrating objects like a talking drum; electrical energy, which flows through wires to power our appliances; chemical energy, stored in food, fuel and batteries; and solar energy, which comes from the sun and can be captured by solar panels common in many Nigerian homes. Each form can be changed into another. Learning to name these forms helps you understand how energy powers everything around you.

What is energy transformation? Give Nigerian examples.

Energy transformation means changing energy from one form to another. Energy is never lost; it simply changes form. Here are everyday Nigerian examples. When you switch on an electric bulb, electrical energy changes into light and heat energy. When a generator runs, chemical energy in the fuel changes into mechanical energy and then electrical energy. When you eat rice and then run, chemical energy in the food changes into mechanical energy in your muscles. At the Kainji Dam, the movement of water (mechanical energy) is changed into electrical energy for homes. When you strike a match, chemical energy becomes heat and light. So look around and you will see energy constantly changing form to do useful work. This idea, that energy only transforms, is a key law of science.

In JSS2 terms, how do potential and kinetic energy differ, with examples?

Potential and kinetic energy are two forms of mechanical energy. POTENTIAL energy is stored energy that an object has because of its position or condition; it is not moving yet, but it could. Examples are a coconut hanging high on a tree, water held behind a dam, and a stretched catapult rubber. KINETIC energy is the energy an object has because it is actually moving. Examples are a falling coconut, flowing river water, and a stone flying from a catapult. Notice how one changes into the other: the hanging coconut has potential energy, but as it falls, that changes into kinetic energy. So the rule is simple: stored and still means potential; moving means kinetic. Watching a swing or a thrown ball, you can see the two swapping back and forth.

What is the main source of energy on earth?

The sun is the main source of energy on earth. Almost all the energy we use can be traced back to the sun. Plants use sunlight to make their food through photosynthesis, and when we or animals eat plants, we get that stored energy. The sun's heat drives the water cycle and the winds, and it dries our crops and clothes. Even fossil fuels like petrol and coal came from plants and animals that lived long ago using the sun's energy. Today we also capture sunlight directly with solar panels to make electricity, which is very useful in areas with poor power supply. So the sun is like a giant free power station in the sky. Without it, there would be no life and almost no energy on earth.
